# Yards First Daily | October 9, 2026

## 1. Executive read

**Most important:** Kodiak and Charger USA are hauling refrigerated and dry freight on a 435-mile Dallas-Laredo lane. The trucks still have safety drivers, and the disclosed operation ends at Laredo. The harder cross-border orchestration begins there.

**Changed since yesterday:** Yesterday’s autonomy signal concerned regulatory permission. Today’s disclosure involves live CPG and food freight, a named carrier, two operating terminals, and a first completed delivery.

**What the market is getting wrong:** Autonomous linehaul mileage is not cross-border execution. Customs, custody, cold-chain state, equipment, and driver handoffs still need one executable instruction.

**Allocation: PUBLISH.** Treat this as a border-handoff story, not another autonomous-truck launch recap.

## 2. Decision-grade signals

### 1. NEW: Kodiak reaches Laredo, but not yet Mexico

**Development:** Kodiak and Charger announced the operation October 8. The first delivery occurred September 8. Kodiak-equipped trucks are moving refrigerated and dry CPG and food-and-beverage freight between Charger terminals in Dallas and Laredo. A safety driver remains behind the wheel; truck count, frequency, customers, and performance are undisclosed. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="0"}

**Why now and buyer read:** This is a live operating deployment, not only a pilot announcement. Charger is combining its proprietary TMS, managed transportation, terminals, and automated-driving supplier. The buying committee therefore spans network operations, safety, terminal operations, cross-border compliance, cold chain, IT, and customers.

**Yard implication: DIRECT.** At Laredo, tractor, trailer, driver, seal, reefer condition, customs status, and Mexico-side capacity must converge before onward release.

**Editorial opportunity:** The autonomous lane ends where the border operating model begins.

**Commercial opportunity:** Charger and other Laredo cross-border carriers; refrigerated networks; CPG and food shippers. Target VP cross-border operations, terminal GM, transportation systems, customs compliance, and food-safety leadership.

**Casey’s move:** Ask Charger: “At Laredo, what event converts the Dallas leg into an authorized Mexico move, and which system owns every exception between trailer arrival and onward release?”

**Score: 28/30, A5 B5 C4 D5 E5 F4. Confidence: HIGH on the supervised operation; LOW on driverless timing and scale.** Primary company disclosure plus independent trade coverage, with no operating metrics.

### 2. NEW: 7-Eleven says it outsourced too much

**Development:** On October 9, 7-Eleven Inc. CEO Mauricio Leyva said the North American business is considering bringing parts of its supply chain in-house while reshaping sourcing and distribution. Seven & i CEO Stephen Dacus said the company had outsourced too much. Longer-term investment is expected to be principally self-funded. No function, site, partner, budget, or deadline was named. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="1"}

**Why now and buyer read:** Management has connected supply-chain ownership to cost reduction and proof of turnaround. The unresolved decision is which capabilities require internal data, labor, assets, or exception authority.

**Yard implication: ADJACENT.** Any change affecting distribution or transportation would alter who controls appointments, inventory availability, trailers, dispatch, and store-service exceptions.

**Editorial opportunity:** Outsourcing transfers work. It does not transfer accountability for physical execution.

**Commercial opportunity:** 7-Eleven first, followed by multi-site convenience and fuel retailers. Target network transformation, distribution operations, transportation, sourcing, finance, and supply-chain systems.

**Casey’s move:** Ask: “Which cost or service failure cannot be fixed while a third party owns the operating data and exception decision?”

**Score: 26/30, A5 B3 C5 D5 E4 F4. Confidence: MEDIUM.** Named CEOs confirm strategic intent, but the physical scope remains undefined.

Source: [Reuters, October 9](https://www.reuters.com/business/7-elevens-us-arm-looks-move-supply-chain-in-house-inflation-bites-2026-10-09/)

### 3. NEW: Metsä returns 260,000 tons of pulsed freight to Philadelphia

**Development:** PhilaPort announced October 8 that Metsä’s return is expected to move approximately **260,000 metric tons annually** through Penn Warehousing’s Forest Products Center. The partnership was celebrated October 7; Wagenborg Shipping will provide sailings every three weeks. :chatgpt-content-reference{index="2"}

**Why now and buyer read:** A recurring cargo commitment now has to become berth, warehouse, labor, truck, and manufacturer capacity. The buying committee includes Metsä, Wagenborg, PhilaPort, Penn Warehousing, labor, drayage, and downstream manufacturers.

**Yard implication: DIRECT.** Annual tonnage arrives in vessel-sized pulses. Floor slots and outbound appointments must be ready before each call.

**Editorial opportunity:** Annual volume hides the operating problem. Capacity must absorb the arrival cadence, not the average.

**Commercial opportunity:** Breakbulk terminals, port warehouses, forest-product importers, and paper or packaging manufacturers. Target terminal operations, warehouse GM, inventory control, drayage, and appointment ownership.

**Casey’s move:** Ask Penn Warehousing which five conditions must be true before each vessel call, and who can reprioritize outbound trucks when one is false.

**Score: 27/30, A4 B5 C4 D5 E4 F5. Confidence: HIGH on volume and cadence; MEDIUM on execution design.**

Source: [PhilaPort announcement](https://www.philaport.com/philaport-welcomes-metsa-back-to-philadelphia/)
